description: Knechtle argues that protective opposition to harm can express love, so divine wrath need not conflict with love and may prevent moral indifference.
critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle explains the contradiction through protective love: opposition to whatever harms a person can express care, while indifference toward wrongdoing would betray it, supporting coherent divine character. Principal limitation: The analogy establishes possibility, not application: no divine punishment is shown to be protective, proportionate, or just, and “a type of Wrath” leaves loving resistance indistinct from punitive violence. Live burden: Since this constructive addresses an anticipated tension rather than an identified opposing move, Knechtle must connect loving anger to contested punishments and demonstrate that they reliably oppose harm without creating harm. Locked score: The mid-seventies outcome reflects stronger coherence, responsiveness, and burden relevance than evidential warrant or calibration, especially because “couldn’t be any more consistent” overstates this comparison.
